items.stem: A pond freezes from the surface downward each winter, and aquatic life survives beneath the ice layer. Which physical property of water: uniquely tied to its molecular geometry, best explains why solid water (ice) is less dense than liquid water?
choices: High specific heat capacity that buffers temperature changes
Strong cohesive forces and surface tension between water molecules
Water's universal solvent property, which prevents close packing of molecules
Hydrogen bonds lock ice into an open lattice that spaces molecules apart
The polar O-H bonds, which orient toward charged ions in solution
items.why: Hydrogen bonds hold ice in an open lattice, so ice is less dense.
steps: In ice, each water makes four hydrogen bonds.
Those bonds fix molecules in an open, hexagonal lattice.
The lattice leaves empty space between molecules.
In liquid, bonds break and reform, so molecules pack closer.
Same mass in more volume: ice is less dense and floats.
traps: Specific heat explains slow temperature change, not why ice floats.
Cohesion explains surface tension. It does not open up the solid.
Solvent power is about dissolving ions. It does not set the density of ice.
Polar bonds turning toward ions describes dissolving, not the ice lattice.

items.stem: A biochemist hydrolyzes an unknown polymer and isolates monomers each composed of a five-carbon sugar, a phosphate group, and a nitrogenous base. Which class of biological macromolecule did the polymer belong to?
choices: Carbohydrate (polysaccharide)
Lipid (triglyceride or phospholipid)
Nucleic acid (DNA or RNA)
Protein (polypeptide)
Glycoprotein (sugar-coated protein)
items.why: Sugar, phosphate and base make a nucleotide, the monomer of nucleic acids.
steps: List the parts: five-carbon sugar, phosphate, nitrogenous base.
Sugar plus phosphate plus base is one nucleotide.
Nucleotides link into DNA or RNA.
So the polymer is a nucleic acid.
traps: Polysaccharides are built from simple sugars only. No phosphate, no base.
Lipids have no repeating monomer that carries a nitrogenous base.
Proteins are built from amino acids, not sugar, phosphate and base.
A glycoprotein is protein plus sugar. It has no nitrogenous bases.

items.stem: Starch and cellulose are both polymers of glucose, yet humans can digest starch but not cellulose. Cattle and termites overcome this limitation only by harboring symbiotic microbes that produce specific cellulases. What molecular feature accounts for this difference in human digestibility?
choices: Cellulose is built from a different monomer than starch, fructose
Cellulose lacks any glycosidic linkages between its glucose units
Starch is hydrophobic, while cellulose is highly hydrophilic
Cellulose monomers are L-glucose, while starch is built from D-glucose
Starch has α-1,4 bonds; cellulose has β-1,4 bonds we cannot cleave
items.why: Starch has α-1,4 links; cellulose has β-1,4 links our enzymes cannot cut.
steps: Both polymers are chains of D-glucose.
Starch joins glucose with α-1,4 bonds.
Cellulose joins glucose with β-1,4 bonds.
Human amylase cuts α bonds only.
Cattle need microbes with cellulase to cut β bonds.
traps: Both are glucose polymers. Cellulose is not made of fructose.
Cellulose has glycosidic bonds. They are β-1,4 instead of α-1,4.
Water attraction is not the issue. The bond type is.
Both use D-glucose. The difference is the α versus β link.

items.stem: When phospholipids are placed in aqueous buffer, they spontaneously self-assemble into a bilayer in which the phosphate-containing head groups face the water and the fatty-acid tails sequester away from it. Which structural feature drives this organization?
choices: All phospholipid molecules are uniformly hydrophobic
The molecule is amphipathic: a polar phosphate head group and two nonpolar fatty-acid tails
Phospholipids covalently bond to surrounding water molecules to form a network
Their fatty-acid tails carry a partial negative charge that repels water
Phospholipids contain ester bonds that hydrolyze rapidly in water
items.why: Phospholipids are amphipathic: a polar head and two nonpolar tails.
steps: The phosphate head is polar and hydrophilic.
The two fatty-acid tails are nonpolar and hydrophobic.
Heads face the water; tails hide from it.
Two layers do this together: a bilayer.
traps: If every part were hydrophobic, no head group would face the water.
No covalent bonds form with water. Tails cluster away from it.
Fatty-acid tails are nonpolar. They carry no partial negative charge.
Ester hydrolysis would break the lipid apart, not organize a bilayer.

items.stem: An enzyme is incubated at 95°C for 5 minutes. The protein loses all catalytic activity but, when re-analyzed by mass spectrometry, retains its original molecular mass and amino-acid sequence. Which level of protein structure has been preserved despite this denaturation?
choices: Secondary structure: α-helices and β-sheets are stabilized by covalent bonds
Tertiary structure: the 3D fold is held only by covalent disulfide bonds
Primary structure: the covalent peptide-bond sequence is unaffected by heat
Quaternary structure: subunit interactions resist heat better than smaller folds
Both tertiary and quaternary, since only secondary structure is heat-sensitive
items.why: Primary structure survives: heat does not break peptide bonds.
steps: Same mass and sequence: the peptide bonds are intact.
Primary structure is that covalent sequence.
Higher levels rely mostly on weak non-covalent forces.
Heat breaks those forces, so the fold and activity are lost.
traps: Helices and sheets are held by hydrogen bonds, not covalent bonds.
The fold relies mostly on weak bonds; disulfides are only part of it.
Subunit contacts are non-covalent, so heat disrupts them too.
Heat disrupts every higher level, not only secondary structure.

items.stem: An mRNA strand contains the sequence 5'-AUGCAU-3'. During reverse transcription using the same mRNA as template, the resulting DNA strand is synthesized as the complement. Which nitrogenous base in the RNA template will pair with adenine on the new DNA strand?
choices: Thymine (T): the standard DNA-DNA pairing partner of adenine
Guanine (G): pairs with cytosine via three H-bonds
Cytosine (C): pairs with guanine, never with adenine
Inosine (I): a modified base in tRNA wobble pairing
Uracil (U): used in RNA in place of thymine
items.why: Uracil in the RNA template pairs with adenine.
steps: RNA uses uracil in place of thymine.
Adenine pairs with thymine in DNA, uracil in RNA.
The template here is RNA, so the partner is U.
traps: Thymine is a DNA base. The template is RNA, which carries uracil.
Guanine pairs with cytosine, not with adenine.
Cytosine pairs with guanine, never with adenine.
Inosine is a tRNA wobble base, not an mRNA template base.

items.stem: A pharmacology student measures the kinetics of an enzyme in the presence of inhibitor X. Adding more substrate fully restores the original Vmax, but the apparent Km has doubled. The Lineweaver-Burk plots of inhibited and uninhibited reactions intersect on the y-axis. What kind of inhibitor is X?
choices: Non-competitive
Competitive
Uncompetitive
Mixed
Allosteric activator
items.why: X is competitive: Vmax is unchanged and the apparent Km rises.
steps: More substrate restores Vmax: the inhibitor is outcompeted.
Km doubled: more substrate is needed for half Vmax.
The plots meet on the y-axis, at 1/Vmax.
Same Vmax with a higher Km means competitive.
traps: Non-competitive lowers Vmax and leaves Km unchanged.
Uncompetitive lowers both Vmax and Km.
Mixed inhibition lowers Vmax as well as shifting Km.
An activator speeds the enzyme up. Km would not double.

items.stem: A microscopist examines two cell types and finds that one has a clearly defined membrane-bound nucleus while the other has DNA distributed in a region called the nucleoid but lacks any internal compartmentalization. Which of the following is uniquely characteristic of EUKARYOTIC cells but absent in PROKARYOTIC cells?
choices: Ribosomes that carry out protein synthesis
A membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles
A plasma membrane separating cytoplasm from environment
DNA used as the hereditary genetic material
Cytoplasm containing dissolved proteins and metabolites
items.why: Only eukaryotes have a membrane-bound nucleus and organelles.
steps: Both cell types have ribosomes, membrane, DNA, cytoplasm.
Prokaryotes keep DNA in a nucleoid, with no membrane.
Eukaryotes wrap DNA in a nuclear envelope.
They also have organelles like mitochondria and Golgi.
traps: Prokaryotes have ribosomes too; theirs are smaller, 70S.
Every cell has a plasma membrane.
Both cell types store their genes in DNA.
All cells have cytoplasm with proteins and metabolites.

items.stem: A pancreatic β cell is secreting insulin. The newly translated insulin precursor passes through the rough ER, undergoes proper folding, and arrives in the next organelle for final modification, including glycosylation, sulfation, and sorting into transport vesicles destined for the plasma membrane. Which organelle handles this final processing and sorting step?
choices: Rough endoplasmic reticulum
Smooth endoplasmic reticulum
Lysosome
Peroxisome
Golgi apparatus
items.why: The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts and packages secreted proteins.
steps: Rough ER makes and folds the protein first.
Vesicles carry it to the Golgi apparatus.
The Golgi adds sugars and other tags.
It sorts the protein into vesicles for the membrane.
traps: Rough ER comes first: synthesis and folding, not final sorting.
Smooth ER makes lipids and detoxifies. It does not sort secretions.
Lysosomes digest material. They do not package secreted proteins.
Peroxisomes break down fatty acids and hydrogen peroxide.

items.stem: A medical technologist places a fresh sample of human red blood cells into a 5% NaCl solution (markedly hypertonic compared to plasma's 0.9% saline) and observes them under a microscope after 30 seconds. Which morphological change is expected?
choices: The cells swell and lyse, releasing hemoglobin into the surrounding medium
The cells remain morphologically unchanged, since RBCs are insensitive to ionic concentration
The cells actively pump in NaCl to equalize osmotic pressure
The cells undergo apoptosis, with characteristic membrane blebbing
The cells shrink and develop a crenated appearance as water flows out by osmosis
items.why: In 5% saline, red cells lose water and shrink (crenation).
steps: 5% NaCl holds more solute than the cell: hypertonic.
Water moves toward the higher solute by osmosis.
Water leaves the cell, so the cell shrinks.
Shrunken red cells look spiky: crenation.
traps: Swelling and lysis happen in hypotonic solution, the opposite case.
Red cells react fast to tonicity; they have no cell wall.
The cell does not pump NaCl in to match. Water moves instead.
Apoptosis is programmed cell death, not a 30 second osmotic change.
